input:
When it comes to temperature measurement, understanding the difference between absolute and relative error is absolutely crucial for anyone who is looking to obtain truly reliable and meaningful results. It is important to note that these two closely related concepts are by no means the same thing, and confusing them can potentially lead to significant misinterpretations further down the line.

Let us consider a simple, concrete example in order to illustrate this important point. Suppose that a temperature instrument gives a reading of 337 units. The instrument in question may well have a stated tolerance of 1% of the reading, which essentially means that the absolute error associated with this particular measurement works out at some 3.37 units. In other words, the absolute error is basically just 1% of 337 units, which gives us our figure of 3.37 units, highlighting just how straightforward the underlying calculation really is.

Relative error, by way of contrast, takes this absolute error and expresses it in relation to the overall size of the measurement itself, thereby providing a dimensionless perspective that can be incredibly useful when measurements of very different magnitudes are being compared with one another. Furthermore, it is also worth noting that error itself should never be confused with uncertainty. Error is fundamentally concerned with the difference between a measured value and the true value, whereas uncertainty is all about the range of values within which the true value might reasonably be expected to fall. Keeping these distinctions clear at all times is, ultimately, essential for robust and reliable measurement practice across the board.
target:
This tutorial explains absolute and relative error through one temperature measurement, and keeps error apart from uncertainty throughout. The measurement reads 337 units. Work through the two forms and the outcome is fixed at the start: the absolute error is 3.37 units, and the relative error is the absolute error divided by the reading.

Absolute error is defined as the difference between a measured value and the true value, stated in the units of the measurement. A tolerance quoted as a percentage of the reading converts directly into an absolute error. Here the tolerance is 1% of the reading, and the absolute error is thus calculated from the reading and the tolerance together: 1% of 337 units is 3.37 units. The sign of the difference is usually dropped in reporting, and the magnitude alone is quoted.

Relative error is defined as the absolute error divided by the measured value. Relative error carries no units, because the units of the numerator and the denominator cancel. A relative error states the size of an error against the size of the quantity measured, so errors on quantities of very different sizes can be compared on one scale.

Error is not uncertainty, and the two terms are not merged in careful reporting. Error is a difference between one measured value and a true value, and error belongs to the single measurement. Uncertainty is a range within which the true value is expected to lie, and uncertainty belongs to the measurement method. A reading can carry a small error and a large uncertainty at the same time.
